title: 2011 Evaluating-Basketball-Player-Performance-via-Statistical-Network-Modeling
universal_lens: Centrality-based statistical inference for player performance evaluation through reference distributions and p-value thresholds. Statistical network modeling integrates player centrality and unit performance to evaluate basketball player efficiency through Bayesian hierarchical inference.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian null hypothesis testing with Benjamini-Hochberg correction applied to centrality-derived p-values for probabilistic player classification. GSI employs Bayesian normal hierarchical models with Gibbs sampling to infer posterior distributions of player efficiencies, enabling probabilistic performance ranking and significance testing across offensive, defensive, and total metrics.
gse_mapping: Situational reasoning engine maps player centrality scores to state transitions between over/under-performance regimes using adjusted p-values as decision metrics. GSE utilizes centrality-based edge scoring to assess teammate synergy and situational impact, supporting dynamic state transitions in player role assignment and tactical decision-making during gameplay.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 3 introduces a statistical framework for evaluating basketball player performance using network-based centrality measures. The core methodology involves constructing reference distributions for each player’s centrality score πi∗ derived from random permutations or simulations. These reference distributions allow comparison of actual player performance πi0 against expected chance performance, yielding p-values. Extreme p-values (either very small or very large) indicate significant deviation from randomness—over-performance or under-performance respectively. The paper employs three distinct networks (offensive, defensive, total efficiency), each containing 590 players across 5961 unique 5-man units. Histograms of raw p-values reveal heavy tails at boundaries, suggesting that extreme performances are more common than uniformity would predict. This observation implies that either exceptional over-performers or under-performers are more prevalent than chance alone would suggest. To address the multiplicity of tests performed across all players, the study applies Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction to control false discovery rate. Adjusted p-values are then used to classify players into over/under-performer categories at a 10% threshold. This approach enables identification of players whose centrality scores deviate significantly from what would be expected by chance, offering actionable insights for team strategy and roster decisions. The framework integrates probabilistic inference with network theory to produce quantifiable performance signals.

The methodology extends beyond individual metrics by incorporating pairwise synergy scoring, assessing how effectively two players collaborate. The core innovation lies in applying a Gibbs sampler to a Bayesian normal hierarchical model, enabling probabilistic inference about player contributions and unit effectiveness. By combining these elements, it provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating basketball players that accounts for both individual and collective contributions.
